html:
Charles Darwin was an English naturalist whose theory of evolution by natural selection explained how all living things descend from common ancestors. He set it out in On the Origin of Species in 1859, and it is now the foundation of biology.

He came from a well off family; one grandfather was the potter Josiah Wedgwood. He dropped out of medicine at Edinburgh and trained for the Church at Cambridge, but his real love was natural history.

The turning point was the voyage of HMS Beagle (1831 to 1836), a survey ship that went around the world. He collected fossils in South America, saw earthquakes raise the land in Chile, and noticed that mockingbirds and tortoises differed from one island of the Galápagos to the next.

The theory, in brief:

  • Living things vary, and some of that variation is inherited.
  • More are born than can survive.
  • Those whose traits suit their surroundings leave more offspring.
  • Over long ages, this natural selection produces new species.

He worked out the idea by 1838, helped by reading Malthus on population, but spent twenty years gathering evidence. In 1858 Alfred Russel Wallace sent him the same idea, and their papers were presented together. The Origin followed the next year and caused a storm, because it left no special place for a divine design. The Descent of Man (1871) applied it to humans.

He did not know how traits were inherited; Mendel's laws, ignored in his lifetime, later supplied that. He is buried in Westminster Abbey, near Isaac Newton.
